newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS-Big powers challenge Indonesia over car.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Big powers challenge Indonesia over car.

text.p: The world's top three trade powers -- the United States, the European Union and Japan -- made clear on Friday they would be mounting a strong challenge against Indonesia's bid to kick-start the launch of a national car.

Officials from the three said they were seeking quick "consultations" with Indonesia on the issue in the first stage of the dispute settlement procedure of the World Trade Organisation, whose rules they say Jakarta is breaking.

EU officials said their request for bilateral talks had been delivered to Indonesia's Geneva mission late on Thursday and Japan followed suit on Friday. A U.S. envoy said the Washington request would probably go in next week.

"We will be throwing the book at them (the Indonesians)," said one diplomat who will be closely involved in the case. "They are trying to drive a coach and horses through the WTO agreements they have signed up to."

There was no immediate comment from the Indonesian mission to the WTO, but Trade and Industry Minister Tunky Ariwibowo said in Jakarta earlier on Friday his country would not back down in the face of big-power pressure.
"Indonesia will not change its car policy. We have a policy and we will implement it and we will not change it on principle," he declared after discussing the issue with President Suharto.

The case will be the first of its significance brought to the 21-month-old WTO by three big powers against a developing country, although all three have been involved in a similar problem with Brazil.
But officials of the three insist they are not "ganging up" on a smaller power, although if as seems certain the dispute goes to a WTO panel, they will link up to present their case.

"This is a matter of principle. The Indonesians are going against so many provisions of the GATT (the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade which is the WTO's underlying pact) that they must be firmly challenged," said another envoy.

Indonesia's national car policy announced earlier this year gives 100 per cent exemptions from tariffs and luxury taxes for three years to PT Timor Putra Nasional which is producing a sedan known as the Timor.
This is seen as unfair discrimination by the big three whose own car companies have a large part of the booming automobile market in Indonesia.

PT Timor, controlled by Suharto's youngest son Hutomo Mandal Putra, plans to begin assembly of the vehicles at home next March and start full manufacturing in 1998. The Timor is currently being made in South Korea and imported.
The company says it plans to build 200,000 units a year by 1998-99 and to have made one million cars before 2003.
But to qualify for the tax concessions, it must reach a local component level of 20 per cent by the first year of production, 40 per cent by the second and 60 per cent the third.

Under WTO rules, Indonesia has 10 days to respond to the consultations request from the three powers and 30 days to start them up. If no accord is reached 30 days after that, the three powers can ask for the creation of a WTO panel.

The initial panel has to deliver its findings within six months, but these can be appealed and the whole process can take well over a year before the WTO's Dispute Settlement Body hands down a final binding ruling.
